reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Madden
bases: A crowd of several hundred attacked the Tiffin jail to seize and lynch a prisoner held for murder and was driven off by an armed posse (A9, A4, A6).
A crowd of several hundred tried to take Madden from the jail to lynch him for a killing he was accused of, but was repelled and he was moved to Toledo unharmed, so no one was killed (A9, A15, A16).

Several independent dispatches from Tiffin, Cincinnati and Toledo describe the attack on the jail (A4, A9, A15, A16), but a Tiffin letter in the Stark County Democrat calls reports of a lynching attempt false (A17).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Charles Madden was an attack by a crowd of several hundred people on the jail at Tiffin, Seneca County, Ohio, early on the morning of November 7, 1881, in an effort to seize and hang Madden, a Heidelberg College student held for the fatal shooting of Phoebe Bernard.
The sheriff's armed posse drove the crowd off after a fight in which two officers were seriously hurt, and Madden was secretly moved to Toledo the next night.
Wire dispatches carried the story across the country, while a Tiffin letter in a newspaper from Madden's home county called the reports of a lynching attempt false.
Madden, whose name was also printed as Madder and Midder, was a student at Heidelberg College in Tiffin who was preparing for the ministry and came from Stark County, Ohio.

On the night of Thursday, November 3, he was accused of shooting Phoebe Bernard on the street near the college after she again refused to marry him; she died almost at once, and he surrendered the next day.

According to a Canton paper, Tiffin was in "a fever of excitement," and his preliminary hearing on Saturday, November 5, was held inside the jail because the authorities feared he would be lynched if taken out.
A dispatch dated Tiffin, November 6, said a crowd had surrounded the jail and threatened to lynch Madden after midnight, and that the sheriff had the militia ready.
According to a special to the Cincinnati Times-Star, a crowd of several hundred came to the jail at 1:30 a.m. on November 7 and demanded the keys.

The sheriff, who had already gathered an armed posse, refused, and in the "lively riot" that followed two officers, named as Brest and Lambertson in one copy and Brisk and Lamberton in another, were badly injured before the crowd was driven back.

Other reports said the jail officers and police repelled the crowd, that several people were wounded, and that warrants were being issued for the leaders while a militia company was called out in case of a second attack.
The crowd gathered again on the night of November 7.

Shortly before midnight the sheriff had Madden quietly taken from the jail, and he then told the crowd it could attack the jail if it wished; another dispatch said the crowd dispersed once it learned the prisoner was gone.
A Tiffin policeman and two assistants took Madden by way of Fremont to Toledo, where he arrived on the morning of November 8 and was hidden in the county jail.
Madden had been bound over for murder in the first degree at his hearing, and the Toledo dispatch expected him to be held there until his trial.
Warrants for the leaders of the crowd were reported, but no report of arrests or prosecutions of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage, and no report of Madden's trial was found.

Nearly all the coverage came from two short wire stories: the Times-Star special, printed with headlines such as "Unsuccessful Attempt at Lynching" in Portland and "Lynchers Routed" in Somerset, Pennsylvania, and a briefer press dispatch that ran from Los Angeles to Arizona.

Papers repeated the name of the accused in several spellings and called him "the murderer" before any trial, while describing the crowd in neutral terms or as "indignant citizens" and "infuriated people."
A Wheeling headline credited "the Ingenuity of a Sheriff" for saving him, and Ohio papers stressed his good standing and possible insanity more than the attack on the jail.
Many papers that reported the shooting, including ones in Mississippi and South Carolina, said nothing about the crowd, and none of the coverage gives a race for Madden, Bernard or the crowd.

The Stark County Democrat, in a Tiffin letter dated November 7, wrote that "sensational reports" of an attempt to lynch Madden "are all false" and that Tiffin people were disposed to let the law take its course.

The same issue of that paper, however, said the hearing was held in the jail for fear of lynching, and dispatches from Tiffin, Toledo and Cincinnati all described an attack on the jail, with injured officers named.

accounts.gist: Several hundred men demanded the jail keys at 1:30 a.m.; the sheriff's armed posse fought them off; two officers were severely injured; warrants were issued and militia ordered out.

accounts.label: Press wire from Tiffin
accounts.gist: Jail officers and police repelled a crowd of several hundred who would have lynched Madden; militia ordered out and warrants issued for ringleaders.

accounts.label: Tiffin dispatch, November 8
accounts.gist: Excitement continued all night; the sheriff moved Madden out before midnight and told the crowd it could attack the jail; the crowd dispersed.

accounts.label: Tiffin letter to the Stark County Democrat
accounts.gist: Reports of an attempt to lynch Madden were 'all false'; Tiffin people were peaceable and willing to let the law take its course.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Times-Star or press dispatch under headlines such as 'Unsuccessful Attempt at Lynching' and 'Lynchers Routed', calling Madden 'the murderer' of Bernard.
Ohio papers called the crowd 'indignant citizens' and 'infuriated people' and the prisoner 'the guilty wretch', while praising the sheriff's ruse.
The Stark County Democrat, from Madden's home county, denied any attempt to lynch him and stressed his standing and possible insanity.

versions.value: A crowd attacked the jail and was repelled; officers injured
Reports of an attempt to lynch Madder 'are all false'

conflicts.note: The denial is a single Tiffin letter; the same paper's own note says the hearing was held in the jail for fear of lynching (A18), and several separate dispatches from Tiffin, Cincinnati and Toledo describe the attack.
The later Eaton Democrat item gives the lower figure.
